title: Redwood cost-econ discovery with Bluehaven Capital
summary: Intro + cost/unit economics deep dive. Customer runs batch scoring and realtime alerts, heavy token volumes for nightly re-runs. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private, per-token economics, batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization tradeoffs, and security requirements (SOC2, KMS, VPC). Agreed to run a short benchmark and get pricing + security pack.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
transcript:
Header: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marcus (Bluehaven), Sophie (Bluehaven), Ethan (Bluehaven)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh i'm jordan with redwood, this is priya our solutions engineer, how's everyone doing?
[00:03] Marcus: good, thanks. we got a compact agenda — want to focus on cost and how you guys think about per token economics.
[00:07] Sophie: yep, timeline is tight; board wants pilot in next quarter.
[00:12] Priya: great; quick show of hands — are you leaning hosted, dedicated or private? or still evaluating?
[00:17] Ethan: leaning hosted for speed but budget is a hard constraint. we do nightly batch runs that are heavy token volumes and some low latency alerts.
[00:23] Jordan: perfect. so we'll run through how batching, kv caching and quantization shift unit cost, and where dedicated/private make sense for predictable throughput and isolation.
[00:31] Marcus: quick thing — are you guys SOC two compliant? we need audit logs and KMS integration.
[00:35] Priya: yes, redwood is SOC 2 and we have KMS/HSM options for private deployments, audit logs in the console. i'll drop the security pack after.
[00:42] Sophie: good. what about data residency? some of our models touch EMEA data.
[00:45] Jordan: we have region routing and private deployments in customer VPCs for residency. note on transcribe: sometimes we see 'v p c' spelled out in our notes, sorry for the auto transcript.
[00:52] Ethan: ok can you walk through numbers — per-token pricing for hosted vs dedicated? and how batching changes it?
[00:58] Priya: rough framework: hosted uses usage-based per-token pricing; dedicated is committed capacity which lowers per-token unit economics for sustained workloads. the key levers are batching (increasing throughput per GPU), kv/prefix caching (avoiding recompute for repeated prefixes), and quantization (lower memory and cheaper kernels).
[01:12] Marcus: example numbers? even ballparks help.
[01:17] Priya: ballpark: for a 3B-ish model hosted might be $0.0006 - $0.0012 per token depending on context length and throughput; with dedicated and good batching you can drop that substantially — we see effective per-token costs 40-70% lower on stable workloads. caching can reduce costs a further 20-50% for repeated prefixes.
[01:36] Marcus: that's broad. for our nightly job: 10M tokens per night across 8 hours, and realtime alerts ~200 qps at peak.
[01:44] Jordan: for the nightly batch you could use dedicated reserved capacity and a higher batch size to maximize GPU utilization; the realtime 200 qps could live on dedicated with autoscale or hosted for bursting. tradeoff: dedicated gives predictable p95 latency targets and lower unit costs, hosted gives simpler ops.
[01:58] Sophie: what's the rollout for private? we have strict compliance and need VPC and KMS plus an on-prem option might be considered.
[02:05] Priya: private gives you customer-managed net and KMS/HSM, audit logs, and can be air-gapped; provisioning timeline depends on infra—typically 6-10 weeks for a VPC private deployment, on-prem longer.
[02:16] Ethan: latency numbers? we can't accept >150ms for alerts.
[02:20] Priya: p50/p95 depends on model and hardware; with dedicated on A100s or equivalent we can hit sub-50ms p50 for short contexts, p95 around 80-120ms depending on batching and KV cache hit rate. hosted SLAs vary by tier.
[02:33] Jordan: quick note on terminology — our internal product names are Redwood Dedicated and Redwood Private, sometimes the transcription shows 'reddwood' or 'red wood' in the notes.
[02:40] Marcus: got it. what about quantized models? do you host quantized variants? any quality regressions?
[02:46] Priya: yes, we support multiple quantization profiles. we always recommend running evals — we have a optimize toolkit that suggests quantization by workload and tracks quality regressions. common pattern: 4-bit quant for throughput-heavy batch scoring with minimal quality delta; we tie evals to prompts so you can validate.
[03:02] Ethan: curious about batching — does batching increase latency for realtime?
[03:07] Priya: batching helps throughput for batch jobs; for realtime we use dynamic batching with latency SLOs plus prefix/KV caching to avoid recompute. you can set routing policies: low-latency requests route to a low-batch path.
[03:19] Sophie: does the KV cache require sticky routing?
[03:23] Priya: No, our KV cache is distributed but cache locality helps; you can pin to nodes if needed. there are tradeoffs — sticky routing improves cache hit rate but reduces flexibility for autoscale.
[03:34] Marcus: examples of customer savings?
[03:37] Jordan: finance customers saw 50% unit cost reductions by moving steady nightly workloads to dedicated + 30% more from caching. another used quantization to cut GPU footprint in half for batch scoring.
[03:50] Ethan: do you have a benchmark worksheet or spreadsheet we can use?
[03:53] Jordan: yes — i'll share our cost-model spreadsheet and a sample benchmark harness. link: https://redwood.link/cost-model (note: placeholder).
[03:59] Marcus: great. procurement question — do you have committed monthly pricing?
[04:03] Jordan: Dedicated is committed/reserved capacity with monthly/annual terms; we can do blended pricing based on usage patterns. Hosted is pay-as-you-go.
[04:12] Sophie: one concern: we have internal quota budgets; what's the ramp risk if our nightly runs double?
[04:16] Priya: autoscaling and burst policies help, but for cost-predictability dedicated with overprovisioning or burst credits is safer. we can model ramp scenarios in the spreadsheet.
[04:27] Marcus: security again — need SAML SSO, RBAC and audit logs.
[04:31] Priya: supported — SSO/SAML, RBAC in the console, audit events exported to your SIEM. we'll include the security whitepaper.
[04:39] Ethan: can you demo a quick trace or token-level cost view?
[04:42] Jordan: sure — priya will show briefly, but we ran out of time for a full console demo.
[04:46] Priya: (screen share simulated) the console has token-level cost, per-route latency, and cache hit metrics; you can set rollout policies and automatic fallback to a cheaper model when quality thresholds are met.
[04:58] Sophie: ok good. next steps?
[05:01] Jordan: recap: we'll send pricing and a pilot proposal, security pack, and benchmark harness. priya will run a quick benchmark with your sample workload if you can grant access to a sanitized data slice.
[05:11] Marcus: we'll provision sample data and give access. timeline: can you get pricing by friday? (2026-03-06)
[05:16] Jordan: yes — i'll get an initial proposal and pricing by 2026-03-06.
[05:20] Ethan: thanks, helpful call.
[05:22] Jordan: thanks everyone.

Notes: transcript contains some mis-terms: 'kv cache' often appears as 'k v cash' or 'K V cache' in auto-transcript; product names sometimes mis-spelled. There was mild crosstalk near 03:50.
